case.case_title: Gunawardena v. Ceylon Petroleum Corporation and Others
case.source_citation: Supreme Court of Sri Lanka, SC (FR) Application No. 28/97, decided on 10 November 2000

clause.text: All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.

case_context.legal_issue: Whether the refusal by the Ceylon Petroleum Corporation to appoint the petitioner as the dealer of a petroleum service station, after the death of the original dealer (the petitioner's father), violated the petitioner's fundamental rights under Article 12(1) of the Constitution.
case_context.petitioner_claim: The petitioner claimed that he had a legitimate expectation to be appointed as the dealer of the service station upon his father's death, having managed the station effectively and efficiently, and that the refusal to appoint him was mala fide, arbitrary, capricious, and violated his right to equal protection under Article 12(1).
case_context.respondent_argument: The respondents argued that the petitioner and his mother operated the station unsatisfactorily with public complaints and irregularities, that the petitioner's application was not properly constituted, that the Marketing Manual was abrogated and not applicable, and that the dealership was lawfully terminated upon the death of the original dealer. They also contended that the matter was a private commercial contract issue not within fundamental rights jurisdiction.
key_facts: The petitioner's father was the dealer of the service station from 1980 until his death in 1996.
The petitioner managed the station before and after his father's death without complaints or defaults.
The petitioner formally applied for dealership after his father's death.
The Corporation appointed another person (11th respondent) as dealer, allegedly bypassing required procedures.
The Marketing Manual required sympathetic consideration to family members of deceased dealers unless incapable of operating the outlet.

reasoning.interpretation_summary: The court held that Article 12(1) requires public authorities to act fairly, reasonably, and without mala fides, even in contractual matters. The petitioner had a legitimate expectation based on the Marketing Manual and his conduct to be considered for appointment. The failure to consider his application fairly and the appointment of another without following procedures violated the petitioner's right to equal protection under the law.
reasoning.application_to_facts: The court found no sufficient evidence supporting the respondents' allegations of unsatisfactory operation or complaints against the petitioner. The Marketing Manual was not abrogated and its provisions applied. The respondents failed to follow the required procedure of considering at least three candidates and giving sympathetic consideration to the petitioner's family. The decision to appoint the 11th respondent was mala fide, arbitrary, and unreasonable, breaching Article 12(1).
principles_established: Public authorities must conform to constitutional requirements under Article 12(1) even in contractual matters.
Legitimate expectation can arise from established procedures and past practices.
Failure to follow fair procedures and mala fide decisions violate the right to equal protection of the law.
Where breach of contract and violation of Article 12(1) arise from the same facts, fundamental rights remedies are available.
precedents_cited: Att. Gen for Hong Kong v. Ng Yuen Shiu (1983) 2 AC 629
Associated Provincial Picture Houses Ltd. v. Wednesbury Corporation (1948) 1 KB 223
Wickrematunga v. Ratwatte and others (1998) 1 Sri LR 201

outcome.holding: The court declared that the petitioner's fundamental rights under Article 12(1) were infringed by the respondents' failure to appoint him as dealer and by the mala fide appointment of the 11th respondent. The court ordered the 1st respondent to pay Rs 250,000 as solatium and Rs 25,000 as costs to the petitioner.
outcome.remedy_or_orders: Declaration of infringement of fundamental rights; payment of Rs 250,000 as solatium and Rs 25,000 as costs by the 1st respondent.

link_explanation.why_this_clause_matters: Article 12(1) was central to the court's reasoning as it protects the petitioner against arbitrary and unfair treatment by a public authority in the exercise of its contractual and administrative functions, ensuring equal protection of the law.

evidence.evidence_excerpt: The court found no evidence of complaints or unsatisfactory operation by the petitioner, noted the Marketing Manual's provisions requiring fair consideration of the petitioner's application, and held the respondents' failure to follow these procedures was mala fide and arbitrary.
